sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: Androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPI), such as enzalutamide and abiraterone, are standard treatments for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). However, a subset of patients display primary resistance and most eventually acquire secondary resistance. This study aimed to define genomic features of ARPI resistance using longitudinal ctDNA analysis.

sec.title: Experimental Design:
sec.p: We used the targeted AR-ctDETECT cell-free DNA (cfDNA) sequencing assay to profile tumor-derived genomic alterations in plasma samples collected at baseline and progression from patients with mCRPC enrolled in the phase III Alliance A031201 trial of first-line enzalutamide with or without abiraterone. Analysis focused on 327 patients with paired samples available from both time points.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Progression plasma samples displayed elevated cfDNA levels and increased ctDNA positivity. AR was the most frequently altered gene at baseline and at progression. AR copy-number gains and AR genomic structural rearrangements (AR-GSR) increased at progression, along with copy-number losses of FANCA, POLD1, RAD54L, CDKN2A, ZNRF3, and ETS2. An AR extrachromosomal DNA signature was enriched at progression and was associated with AR-GSRs predicted to truncate the AR ligand-binding domain. Stratification by two extre mes of radiographic progression-free survival revealed preferential accumulation of AR alterations in patients with delayed progression and a higher burden of non-AR alterations in patients with rapid progression.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: AR alterations in ctDNA accumulate at progression in patients with mCRPC treated with ARPIs, especially in those with initially durable responses. These findings support the use of liquid biopsy to serially track resistance mechanisms and inform precision therapy in advanced prostate cancer.

boxed-text.p: Current management of metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) lacks tools to assess primary and acquired resistance to androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPI). This study demonstrates the value of longitudinal ctDNA analysis in identifying AR-driven and non–AR-driven resistance mechanisms using plasma specimens from a phase III trial of ARPI therapy. AR was the most frequently altered gene at baseline and at progression, particularly in patients with acquired resistance. An AR extrachromosomal DNA signature defined by concurrent AR copy-number gain and multiple AR rearrangements increased at progression and was associated with the accumulation of AR rearrangements predicted to truncate the AR ligand-binding domain. Conversely, patients with primary resistance displayed a high burden of non-AR genetic alterations. These findings highlight the clinical utility of liquid biopsy for capturing genomic evolution and distinguishing patients with differing mechanisms of treatment resistance, providing a framework for future biomarker-driven precision therapy in mCRPC.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Prostate cancer is the most commonly diagnosed malignancy and the second leading cause of cancer-related death among men in the United States (1). Most prostate cancer tumors rely on androgens and androgen receptor (AR) driven transcriptional activity for growth and survival (2). Accordingly, androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) remains the foundation of first-line treatment for advanced disease. However, resistance to ADT inevitably develops, resulting in progression to a lethal stage known as metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). Although AR pathway inhibitors (ARPI) such as enzalutamide (ENZ) and abiraterone acetate have extended survival in mCRPC (3, 4), 20% to 40% of patients exhibit primary resistance and most eventually acquire secondary resistance (2, 5). Understanding the mechanisms driving both primary and acquired resistance to ARPIs is critical for developing more effective treatment strategies, particularly in earlier hormone-sensitive settings in which these ARPIs are more commonly used and even more effective at delaying progression and improving survival (6–10).

Despite castrate levels of circulating androgens, AR-driven transcriptional activity remains active in most mCRPC cases (2, 5). This persistent AR activity is frequently driven by alterations in the AR gene, including copy-number gains in the AR gene body or AR enhancer, activating point mutations and genomic structural rearrangements (AR-GSR; refs. 11–13). Certain AR-GSRs truncate the ligand-binding domain (LBD) of AR protein and promote the expression of constitutively active AR variants (AR-V) such as AR-V7, which are associated with poor outcomes (13–18). In some tumors, AR copy-number gains and AR-GSRs co-evolve on extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), leading to numerous structurally diverse copies of the AR gene in individual CRPC cells (19, 20). Although AR alterations are central to mCRPC biology, additional recurrent genomic alterations shape disease trajectory and therapeutic response. For example, loss of TP53, RB1, or PTEN can promote AR-independent progression and lineage plasticity, especially when these alterations co-occur (12, 21). Additionally, alterations in DNA repair and mismatch repair pathways are clinically actionable, conferring sensitivity to PARP inhibitors (22) or immune checkpoint blockade (23), respectively.

Identifying these genetic alterations typically requires tumor biopsy and DNA sequencing (DNA-seq). However, metastatic lesions, particularly in the bone, may be inaccessible and exhibit spatial and temporal heterogeneity. Therefore, tumor sampling is generally impractical for longitudinal disease monitoring, highlighting the need for minimally invasive approaches that can capture dynamic changes in tumor genetics. Liquid biopsies, including analysis of ctDNA in plasma-derived cell-free DNA (cfDNA), offer a promising strategy for monitoring genomic evolution and treatment resistance in mCRPC (24).

The AR-ctDETECT assay is a targeted cfDNA sequencing platform that targets 820 kb across 69 genes recurrently altered in mCRPC. By combining genome-wide measures of ctDNA aneuploidy with high-confidence mCRPC-specific alterations, including AR alterations, this assay enables sensitive detection of ctDNA from low-input plasma samples. In a previous study, we applied AR-ctDETECT to 776 baseline plasma samples from the phase III Alliance A031201 trial (NCT01949337), in which patients with first-line mCRPC were randomized to ENZ or ENZ plus abiraterone acetate and prednisone (ENZ + AAP; ref. 25). In that cohort, detection of ctDNA at baseline was prognostic for more rapid disease progression and death (26), and ctDNA alterations were used to build a clinical–genomic prognostic model for overall survival (OS) that improved on a clinically validated prognostic model that used clinical variables only (27).

In the current study, we applied AR-ctDETECT to 431 plasma specimens collected at progression from the A031201 trial. All 776 baseline and 431 progression samples were processed using a standardized pipeline, yielding a set of 327 patients with matched baseline and progression data for direct longitudinal comparisons of cfDNA and ctDNA features under ARPI treatment pressure. At progression, we observed increased cfDNA yield and ctDNA positivity, consistent with the enrichment of features previously linked to poor prognosis. AR copy-number gains and AR-GSRs accumulated at progression, with their co-occurrence reflecting an AR ecDNA signature that was associated with the enrichment of LBD-truncating AR-GSRs. Additionally, we identified increased frequencies of copy-number losses in genes involved in DNA repair, cell cycle control, and transcriptional regulation. Finally, comparison of two extremes of clinical response revealed that AR alterations accumulated in patients with delayed radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS), whereas non-AR alterations were enriched in patients with rapid rPFS. These findings suggest that distinct genomic trajectories underlie primary versus acquired ARPI resistance in mCRPC.

sec.title: Ethics statement
sec.p: This study was approved by the University of Minnesota Institutional Review Board on 09/29/2020 (STUDY00010929), the Duke University Institutional Review Board on 09/23/2020 (Pro00106740), and the NCI Clinical Trials Network for correlative science proposal CSC0159 on 06/16/2021 in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Only plasma from patients who provided written informed consent for blood studies was used.

sec.title: Patients and plasma samples
sec.p: Plasma samples were obtained from patients in the Alliance A031201 clinical trial (Clinicaltrials.gov: NCT01949337) comparing the efficacy of ENZ + AAP vs ENZ in the first-line mCRPC setting (25). Eligible patients had previously untreated mCRPC and/or progressive metastatic disease despite receiving ADT. Patients who had received prior docetaxel or first-generation AR inhibitors were eligible to participate in the trial. Other study details, including study endpoints, inclusion criteria, and specimens collected, have been published (25). Receipt of banked pretreatment (baseline) EDTA plasma samples from the Alliance biorepository at The Ohio State University was described in our previous study (26). As for the baseline samples, 2 to 3 mL EDTA plasma samples collected from patients at progression were shipped on dry ice from the Alliance biorepository at The Ohio State University to the University of Minnesota. Only samples having at least 2 mL of EDTA plasma available were included to avoid exhausting the biorepository.

sec.title: cfDNA isolation and quantification
sec.p: cfDNA was isolated from 2 to 3 mL EDTA plasma progression samples (mean input = 2.29 mL, SD = 0.46 mL) using QIAamp Circulating Nucleic Acid Kit (QIAGEN #55114) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. DNA was eluted in 30 μL of elution buffer. cfDNA concentration was measured using 3 μL of input using Qubit 1x dsDNA HS Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific #Q33231) and a Qubit Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific #Q33216, RRID: SCR_020553). cfDNA yield was calculated as total eluted cfDNA mass divided by plasma input volume.

sec.title: Targeted cfDNA sequencing
sec.p: Progression cfDNA samples with masses of at least 1 ng were used as input for DNA-seq library preparation using ThruPLEX Plasma-seq Kit (Takara #R400681) with Takara Bio DNA Unique Dual Index Kit tubes A (Takara #R400665), B (Takara #R400666), C (Takara #R400667), and D (Takara #R400668). Library cleanup, amplification, and targeted DNA-seq using the AR-ctDETECT assay were performed as previously described (26). Targeted DNA-seq was performed at the University of Minnesota Genomics Center using an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 SP (RRID: SCR_016387) flow cell with 2 × 150 bp settings.

sec.title: DNA-seq read mapping and duplicate removal
sec.p: Raw DNA-seq data from all baseline (26) and progression cfDNA samples were processed using the AR-ctDETECT analysis pipeline as previously described (26). Briefly, read-trimming was performed on FASTQ files using Trimmomatic (v. 0.39, RRID: SCR_011848; ref. 28). Reads were mapped to the GRCh37/hg19 human reference genome using Burrows-Wheeler Aligner MEM (v. 0.7.17; http://arxiv.org/abs/1303.3997). samblaster (v. 0.1.24, RRID: SCR_000468) was used to limit the number of split alignments for a read (max = 2) and limit the number of nonoverlapping base pairs between two alignments (min = 20). Duplicate reads were marked and removed from BAM files using Picard MarkDuplicates (v. 2.25.5, RRID: SCR_006525; https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/) with default settings.

sec.title: Estimation of ctDNA aneuploidy fraction
sec.p: ctDNA aneuploidy fraction was estimated using ichorCNA (v.0.2.0, RRID: SCR_024768; ref. 29) in R (v.4.2.0, RRID: SCR_001905) using off-target reads in duplicate-removed BAM files as the input (https://github.com/GavinHaLab/ichorCNA_offtarget; ref. 30). Details of on-target read removal and genome-wide binned read counting prior to ichorCNA, as well as the ichorCNA settings used for calculating ctDNA aneuploidy fraction, have been described (26).

sec.title: Single-nucleotide variant /indel calling and filtering
sec.p: Single-nucleotide variant (SNV)/indel calling was performed on duplicate-removed BAM files using Freebayes (v.1.3.1, RRID: SCR_010761; http://arxiv.org/abs/1207.3907) and GATK MuTect2 (v.4.1.6.0, RRID: SCR_000559; ref. 31) with settings that have been described (26). SNV/indels were retained if they were identified by both Freebayes and MuTect2 and met the following criteria: (i) the variant was labeled oncogenic or likely oncogenic by Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (v. 104.3, RRID: SCR_007931; ref. 32) and curated in OncoKB (v. 3.3.1, RRID: SCR_014782; ref. 33) or (ii) if the variant was not curated in OncoKB, it must have been labeled oncogenic or likely oncogenic by Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor but must also not have had a splice-site or splice-region classification in OncoKB. Additional filtering criteria were applied for assay-targeted genes based on known nonpathogenic and/or germline variant status: PMS2 (remove p.Arg20Gln); MET (remove p.Glu168Asp); KMT2C (remove p.Tyr816Ter); ATM (remove p.His1380Tyr); FANCA (remove p.Ser1088Phe and p.Ser858Arg); NCOR1 (remove p.Arg190Ter); AURKA (remove p.Phe31Ile); and FOXA1 (ignore OncoKB filtering above and remove all synonymous mutations, p.Ala83Thr, p.Ser448Asn, and p.Leu148Val). Final filtered variants were classified as likely germline if they affected HSD3B1 or any gene other than AR, TP53, PTEN, ERF, PIK3CA, or CDK12 with a variant allele frequency (VAF) between 0.45 to 0.55 and >0.95. The remaining filtered SNVs/indels were classified as likely somatic.

sec.title: Sample matching with NGSCheckMate
sec.p: NGSCheckMate (RRID: SCR_022994; ref. 34) was used to evaluate single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) in the Freebayes variant call format (VCF) files from the 334 pairs of baseline and progression cfDNA samples with identical patient IDs. Dendrogram outputs were manually inspected to identify 327 true matches between baseline and progression cfDNA sample pairs. The baseline cfDNA samples that were identified as unmatched were OM33117 (SUBJ215), OM19377 (SUBJ25), OM67407 (SUBJ825), OM50806 (SUBJ471), OM24844 (SUBJ65), OM73876 (SUBJ927), and OM65235 (SUBJ763). The progression cfDNA samples that were identified as unmatched were OM67432_P (SUBJ215), OM59854_P (SUBJ25), OM61607_P (SUBJ65), OM84163_P (SUBJ825), OM86376_P (SUBJ471), OM97157_P (SUBJ927), and OM97157_P (SUBJ763). These samples were removed from the patient-matched cohort.

sec.title: Identification of gene-specific copy-number alterations
sec.p: Read depths were calculated by mosdepth (v. 0.3.3, RRID: SCR_018929) at every position targeted by the capture panel (i.e., gene exons or control regions) using the duplicate-removed BAM file as the input with no limit on the number of reads counted. Default parameters were used, except –fast-mode and –flag 1796, which discarded unmapped, secondary, quality control–, or duplicate reads from the read depth sum at every position. Within-sample normalized read depths were calculated for each gene relative to five control regions as described (26). Copy-number ratios for each gene X were determined by comparing the normalized read depth for gene X in every sample Y against the average normalized read depth for gene X determined from 71 baseline or progression samples with tumor fraction ≤0.05 (determined by ichorCNA) using the following calculation: copy-number ratio = norm_read_depth for gene X in sample Y/mean (norm_read_depth for gene X in 71 samples with tumor fraction ≤0.05). Genes were classified as having a copy-number gain if log2 (copy-number ratio) > 0.3 and a copy-number loss if the log2 (copy-number ratio) < −0.3, and the sample was classified as ctDNA-positive.

sec.title: Identification and classification of AR-GSRs and AR ecDNA signatures
sec.p: AR-GSRs were called from structural variants identified using Manta (v.1.5.0, RRID: SCR_022997; ref. 35), Delly (v.0.8.1, RRID: SCR_004603; ref. 36), SvABA (v.1.1.0, RRID: SCR_022998; ref. 37), and lumpy (v.0.3.0, RRID: SCR_003253; ref. 38) with input files, settings, and filtering parameters as previously described (26). AR-GSRs were classified as structural variants if identified by at least two of the four SV callers, with at least three supporting split reads and three supporting discordant paired-end reads, having at least one breakend intersecting the AR gene region. Each AR-GSR was evaluated for whether it was likely to encode an AR variant with a truncated LBD. Criteria for inclusion in this list of likely LBD-truncating AR-GSRs include: (i) a deletion (DEL), inversion (INV), or unresolved rearrangement (BND) that fully or partially overlaps AR exons 4, 5, 6, and 7 and/or the start of exon 8 through the stop codon of exon 8 but does not overlap the interval spanning the beginning of AR exon 1 through the end of AR exon 3; (ii) a duplication (DUP), INV, or BND that fully overlaps the interval from the start of AR exon 1 through the end of AR exon 3 with a breakend anywhere between the end of AR exon 3 and the stop codon in AR exon 8; (iii) a DUP with both start and end breakends within the AR gene and flanking one or more of AR exons 3 to 7; or (iv) a translocation with a breakend anywhere between the end of AR exon 3 and the stop codon in AR exon 8 that retains the centromeric side of AR encompassing exons 1 to 3. Samples with AR-GSRs were classified as likely containing AR ecDNA if that sample contained multiple (2 or more) AR-GSRs and displayed copy-number gain of the AR gene body, defined as log2 (copy-number ratio) > 0.3.

sec.title: Definition of ctDNA-positive cfDNA samples
sec.p: The mean ctDNA aneuploidy fraction calculated from AR-ctDETECT assays (n = 13) performed on control cfDNA isolated from a pool of plasma from healthy male donors (Zen-Bio, Inc., #SER-PDP-10) was 0.0749 with an SD of 0.0322. Samples exceeding the mean +2 SD (>0.1394) were classified as ctDNA-positive (group 1). Samples below this threshold were classified as ctDNA-positive if they contained at least one of the following: a likely somatic SNV in any gene targeted by the AR-ctDETECT assay; AR log2(copy-number ratio) > 0.3; AR enhancer log2 (copy-number ratio) > 0.3; AR-GSR detected; MYC log2 (copy-number ratio) > 0.3; and MYCN log2 (copy-number ratio) > 0.3 (group 2). The remaining samples were classified as ctDNA-negative (group 3).

sec.title: OncoPrints
sec.p: Genetic alterations in ctDNA-positive baseline and progression samples for the fast- and slow-progressor groups were organized in an OncoPrint using the cBioPortal data visualization tool (RRID: SCR_014555; refs. 39, 40).

sec.title: Data analysis
sec.p: The analysis included 327 paired samples from patients with specimens collected at both baseline and progression time points. Samples were categorized by ctDNA status and by the time of collection (baseline or progression). To evaluate within-patient changes in continuous variables, we used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (41). For paired binary outcomes, McNemar’s test (42) was applied to assess changes in the proportions between the two time points and then adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Specifically, McNemar’s test was first used to assess individual classes of AR gene alterations and then subsequently used to assess alterations consolidated for all genes in the AR-ctDETECT assay. In addition, differences in unpaired binary outcomes, including ctDNA LBD-truncating alterations and ctDNA status, were analyzed using a generalized estimating equation model (43) to account for within-patient correlation. All P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control the FDR (44). In clinical practice, rapid progression within 6 months in this first-line setting is considered a duration consistent with minimal clinical benefit, meaning that the patient is progressing despite ARPI therapy at their first or second imaging interval (3, 4). This group was chosen as a rapid progression group for exploratory analysis of genetic alterations associated with primary ARPI resistance. Based on the observed median rPFS in A031201 being 21.3 [95% confidence interval (CI), 19.4–22.9] months for ENZ versus 24.3 (95% CI, 22.3–26.7) months for ENZ + AAP (25), we a priori defined a delayed progression subgroup (those clearly having better outcomes and deriving significant clinical benefit) prospectively as those with an rPFS of greater than 30 months. This provides a balance of having an adequate sample size for exploratory analysis and a subgroup clearly experiencing long-term clinical benefits from first-line ADT/ARPI therapy beyond just the median outcome.

sec.title: Longitudinal analysis of A031201 plasma reveals increased cfDNA and ctDNA at progression
sec.p: The Alliance A031201 clinical trial randomized 1,311 patients to ENZ or ENZ + AAP as a first-line therapy for mCRPC (Supplementary Table S1). Although ENZ + AAP did not improve OS compared with ENZ alone, the combination modestly delayed the secondary endpoint of rPFS by 3 months (25). Of the 1,311 patients, 1,059 provided consent for blood studies, and 509 had plasma collected at disease progression and stored in a biorepository. cfDNA was isolated from 432 of these patients with at least 2 mL of progression plasma in the biorepository, and cfDNA was successfully detected in 431 of these. Patients with less than 2 mL of progression plasma (n = 77) were excluded to avoid exhausting any patient plasma in the biorepository, per Alliance policy. Targeted paired-end DNA-seq was performed on the 431 progression cfDNA specimens using the research-grade AR-ctDETECT assay (see CONSORT diagram; Fig. 1A; Supplementary Table S2; ref. 26).

sec.p: In a previous study (26), we used AR-ctDETECT to analyze cfDNA from 776 baseline plasma samples collected prior to treatment in the Alliance A031201 trial. Based on patient identifiers, 334 patients had cfDNA-seq data available from both baseline and progression time points (Fig. 1B). We used NGSCheckMate to compare germline SNPs and confirm genetic matches between samples (34). Of the 334 baseline-progression pairs with matching patient identifiers, 327 (98%) were confirmed by NGSCheckMate, indicating a high level of sample concordance (Fig. 1B). To minimize sampling bias and ensure consistency in cohort composition between baseline and progression samples, analyses were restricted to these 327 patients with matched cfDNA data at both time points (Supplementary Data S1).

In this cohort of 327 patients with matched samples, the median time from study enrollment to rPFS endpoint was 16.5 months, and the median interval between baseline and progression plasma collections was 11.2 months (Supplementary Fig. S1). The 16.5-month median rPFS in the matched cfDNA cohort is notably shorter than the median rPFS in the full trial arms (21.3 months for ENZ; 24.3 months for ENZ + AAP). This is likely because our requirement for patients with matched cfDNA data at both time points excluded all patients who lacked disease progression during the trial. Progression plasma samples had a higher cfDNA yield than baseline plasma samples (Fig. 1C; Supplementary Data S2), corresponding with higher mean unique read coverage of gene regions targeted by the AR-ctDETECT assay (Fig. 1D). This increase was driven primarily by a greater number of patients having a net positive change in cfDNA yield at progression than patients having a net negative change (Fig. 1E). We calculated ctDNA aneuploidy fraction using a modification of the ichorCNA algorithm that only considers off-target reads from the AR-ctDETECT assay (26). The median ctDNA aneuploidy fraction was 12.1% at baseline (range 0.7%–84.6%) and 12.8% at progression (range of 5%–85.6%; Supplementary Fig. S2A, Supplementary Data S2), which positively correlated with cfDNA yield at both time points (Supplementary Fig. S2B and S2C).

Samples were classified as ctDNA-positive as described previously (26), based on exceeding a ctDNA aneuploidy fraction threshold derived from pooled normal male donor plasma, or falling below this threshold but harboring a detectable pathogenic mutation, an AR-GSR, and/or copy-number gain in AR, MYC, or MYCN. Several pathogenic mutations occurred in TP53, ATM, CHEK2, BRCA1, and BRCA2, which are genes that can be mutated in clonal hematopoiesis (CH; ref. 45). Because CH and prostate cancer are influenced by increased age, samples containing these mutations could be false-positive for ctDNA. Therefore, we evaluated whether samples with these potential CH mutations had additional evidence to support them as being ctDNA-positive. Of the 327 paired samples, only 14 (4.3%) baseline samples and 8 (2.4%) progression samples were classified as ctDNA-positive based on a potential CH mutation alone, indicating a low potential for false-positivity caused by CH (Supplementary Fig. S3A and S3B).

Using the above definitions for ctDNA positivity, the proportion of ctDNA-positive samples increased from 62% at baseline to 77% at progression (Fig. 1F). To investigate this further, we categorized patients by their ctDNA status at both time points. Among the 327 sample pairs, 167 (51.1%) were ctDNA-positive at both baseline and progression, 37 (11.3%) converted from ctDNA-positive to ctDNA-negative, 85 (26.0%) converted from ctDNA-negative to ctDNA-positive, and 38 (11.6%) remained ctDNA-negative at both time points (Fig. 1G). Most patients who converted to ctDNA-negative exhibited a decrease in ctDNA aneuploidy fraction at progression, whereas the majority of those who converted to ctDNA-positive displayed an increase (Fig. 1G). However, patients who were ctDNA-positive at both baseline and progression did not seem to exhibit consistent increases in ctDNA aneuploidy fraction. Collectively, these results demonstrate increased plasma cfDNA levels and rates of ctDNA positivity at progression in A031201 patients with mCRPC.

sec.title: Longitudinal analysis of A031201 ctDNA reveals accumulation of AR gene alterations at progression
sec.p: AR was the most frequently altered gene in ctDNA-positive samples (Supplementary Data S3–S5). To characterize AR alterations that may evolve during disease progression, we evaluated copy-number gain of the AR gene body, copy-number gain of the upstream AR enhancer, AR-GSRs, and pathogenic AR SNVs separately. These alterations were detected across all ctDNA-positive specimens, including baseline specimens that later became ctDNA-negative, and progression specimens that converted from ctDNA-negative to ctDNA-positive (Fig. 2A–E). To minimize noise from variable ctDNA detectability and enable reliable longitudinal comparisons, analyses of changes in genetic alterations were restricted to the 167 paired patients who were ctDNA-positive at both time points.

Split reads were normalized by dividing the split read count by the ctDNA aneuploidy fraction of the corresponding sample. The Mann–Whitney U test was used to analyze the difference between both groups. Solid horizontal lines on violins indicate means, whereas the dashed horizontal lines represent upper and lower quartiles. K, Bar graphs showing the cumulative counts of AR-GSRs in n = 167 patients positive for ctDNA at both baseline and progression.

sec.p: In this subset of 167 paired patients, the most prevalent AR alterations at baseline were copy-number gains in the AR gene body (49.7%) and AR enhancer (50.9%), both of which increased at progression to 62.3% and 64.1%, respectively (Fig. 2F). There was substantial overlap between patients with AR gene body gain and patients with AR enhancer gain. More patients displayed copy-number increases in the AR gene body and AR enhancer than decreases (Supplementary Fig. S4A and S4B). The observed increases did not seem to be explained by increased ctDNA aneuploidy fraction (Supplementary Fig. S4C and S4D), indicating that AR and AR enhancer copy numbers increased at progression in the majority of patients. AR-GSRs were also prevalent, increasing from 37.1% at baseline to 58.1% at progression (Fig. 2F). Notably, AR-GSRs represented the most frequent AR alteration at baseline in the 35 ctDNA-positive patients that converted to ctDNA-negative at progression, as well as at progression in the 85 patients in whom ctDNA emerged at progression (Supplementary Table S3). In contrast, pathogenic AR SNVs remained infrequent, occurring in 4.2% of baseline ctDNA and 4.8% of progression ctDNA (Fig. 2F). Among these 167 patients, only three displayed the same AR SNV at both time points (Fig. 2E). The other five patients with AR SNVs at progression did not display the corresponding AR SNV at baseline. We also noted two patients that harbored two AR SNVs concurrently at progression. Four patients harbored AR SNVs at baseline that were not detected at progression. To investigate these patterns in more detail, we manually inspected DNA-seq reads from all 12 patients with AR SNVs at either time point. In cases in which the same AR SNV was detected at both time points, VAFs were similar (Supplementary Fig. S5A–S5C). Of the AR SNVs present at baseline but not at progression, three did display DNA-seq reads to support their persistence at progression but at VAFs below assay cutoffs (Supplementary Fig. S5D–S5F), whereas the remaining one displayed insufficient read depth for detection in the progression sample (Supplementary Fig. S5G). Of the AR SNVs that were only detected at progression, one showed low-level presence at baseline (Supplementary Fig. S5H), whereas five seemed to be newly acquired (Supplementary Fig. S5H–S5L). Collectively, these data suggest that the low frequency and stochastic longitudinal detection of AR SNVs make them less consistent contributors to disease evolution, whereas AR gene body/enhancer copy-number gains and AR-GSRs are the predominant AR alterations enriched at progression in A031201 patients with mCRPC.

sec.title: LBD-truncating AR-GSRs and AR ecDNA signatures co-accumulate at progression
sec.p: We pursued the observation that AR-GSRs were more prevalent at progression in patient-matched samples. Certain AR-GSRs have been shown to alter AR mRNA splicing and drive expression of truncated, constitutively active AR-Vs such as AR-V7, which lack the C-terminal LBD of AR protein (13–18). This is clinically significant because detection of AR-V7 in circulating tumor cells is associated with shorter PFS and OS in mCRPC (46), and our prior analysis of Alliance A031201 baseline ctDNA demonstrated that detection of LBD-truncating AR-GSRs is also associated with shorter rPFS and OS (26). To investigate this relationship further, we categorized AR-GSRs detected in patient-matched samples as either predicted to truncate the AR LBD or of unknown significance (Fig. 2D; Supplementary Data S6). Among the 167 paired patients who were ctDNA-positive at both time points, the prevalence of LBD-truncating AR-GSRs increased from 6.0% at baseline to 24.6% at progression (Fig. 2G). Deletions affecting the 3’ end of the AR gene that remove one or more LBD-encoding exons (exons 5–8) were not detected at baseline in patient-matched samples but appeared at progression (Fig. 2H). All other structural patterns of LBD-truncating AR-GSRs were detectable at baseline and showed increased frequency at progression (Fig. 2H).

AR-GSRs with structural patterns of unknown significance were also observed in patient-matched baseline samples and showed increased prevalence at progression (Fig. 2H). However, when we analyzed the DNA-seq read support to approximate their VAFs, AR-GSRs with structural patterns of unknown significance had lower numbers of supporting DNA-seq split reads than LBD-truncating AR-GSRs, even when the split reads were normalized to the ctDNA aneuploidy fraction (Fig. 2I and J). This indicates that LBD-truncating AR-GSRs are clonally enriched relative to AR-GSRs of unknown significance and suggests that baseline absences are likely due to differences in detection sensitivity influenced by clonal enrichment as opposed to true absences at baseline.

In a previous study, we identified AR amplification on ecDNA as a mechanism driving high AR copy-number gains and accumulation of complex AR-GSRs in individual mCPRC cells (19). In our previous analysis of baseline samples from Alliance A031201, we defined a surrogate AR ecDNA signature as the presence of AR copy-number gain concurrent with two or more AR-GSRs (19) and found that this signature was associated with shorter rPFS and OS duration (26). Consistent with these prior findings, the prevalence of the AR ecDNA signature increased from 11.4% at baseline to 28.7% at progression in the 167 patients who were ctDNA-positive at both time points (Fig. 2G).

We further investigated the co-enrichment of LBD-truncating AR-GSRs and AR ecDNA signatures at progression. Among the 97 patients positive for AR-GSRs at progression, the average number of AR-GSRs per patient was 3.33 compared with 2.44 among the 62 patients with AR-GSRs at baseline (Fig. 2K). This increase is consistent with previous work showing that AR ecDNA promotes the accumulation of complex AR-GSRs in addition to high-level AR amplification (19). Supporting this, the majority of the AR-GSRs that emerged at progression occurred in ctDNA-positive samples that also harbored the AR ecDNA signature (Fig. 3A and B). This pattern was especially pronounced for LBD-truncating AR-GSRs (Fig. 3A), suggesting that AR ecDNA may underlie their preferential accumulation. To test this, we analyzed ctDNA-positive progression samples with AR-GSRs and found that LBD-truncating AR-GSRs were more frequent in samples exhibiting an AR ecDNA signature compared with those lacking this signature (Fig. 3C). These findings support a model in which AR ecDNA promotes the accumulation of LBD-truncating AR-GSRs under therapeutic pressure from ARPIs in mCRPC.

sec.p: Because multiple AR-GSRs can accumulate on individual AR ecDNA molecules (19), we reasoned that a subset of AR-GSRs with unknown significance but unexpectedly high VAF could potentially be explained by their co-occurrence on the same AR ecDNA molecules that harbor LBD-truncating AR-GSRs. In support of this, AR-GSRs with unknown significance had higher numbers of raw and normalized supporting DNA-seq split reads, signifying higher VAFs, if they co-occurred in samples with AR-GSRs that were predicted to truncate the AR LBD (Fig. 3D and E).

sec.title: Longitudinal analysis of A031201 ctDNA reveals accumulation of copy-number losses in non-AR genes at progression
sec.p: To identify tumor-derived, non-AR genetic alterations associated with disease progression, we assessed the frequency of pathogenic SNVs in the additional 68 genes included in the AR-ctDETECT assay (Supplementary Table S2). Among the 167 patients who were ctDNA-positive at both baseline and progression, no individual gene displayed a significant change in pathogenic SNV frequency over time (Fig. 4A; Supplementary Data S2). However, when SNVs and copy-number alterations (CNA) were consolidated, several genes exhibited significantly higher alteration frequencies in progression samples. These included genes involved in DNA repair and replication: FANCA (23.3% at baseline vs. 40.1% at progression), ERCC3 (13.8% vs. 25.1%), RAD54L (12.6% vs. 26.3%), POLE (5.4% vs. 14.4%), and POLD1 (4.5% vs. 21.0%); negative regulation of cell cycle and Wnt signaling: CDKN2A (17.4% vs. 34.1%) and ZNRF3 (13.8% vs. 29.3%); and ETS2 (14.4% vs. 29.9%), a transcription factor that functions as a prostate tumor-suppressor (Fig. 4B; refs. 47–49). These alterations were predominantly copy-number losses (Fig. 4C), which was consistent with frequent heterozygous losses observed in these genes in a separate analysis of the Stand Up To Cancer West Coast mCRPC biopsy dataset (Fig. 4D). Together, these findings demonstrate that ctDNA from A031201 patients captures recurrent genomic alterations found in mCRPC tissue and that longitudinal ctDNA analysis can reveal the emergence of non-AR alterations that may underlie acquired resistance to ARPIs by impairing DNA repair, cell-cycle regulation, and transcriptional control.

sec.title: A031201 treatment arms display comparable ctDNA features at progression
sec.p: To investigate whether treatment regimen influenced cfDNA characteristics or genomic alterations in ctDNA at progression, we stratified progression cfDNA samples by treatment group. cfDNA yields, the proportion of ctDNA-positive samples, and ctDNA aneuploidy fractions were all comparable between patients treated with ENZ alone and those treated with ENZ + AAP (Supplementary Fig. S6A–E). Similarly, the frequency of genomic alterations across the 69-gene AR-ctDETECT panel did not differ between treatment arms (Supplementary Fig. S6F). These results indicate that patients receiving ENZ alone or dual AR blockade with ENZ + AAP exhibit similar cfDNA and ctDNA profiles at progression.

sec.title: Non-AR ctDNA alterations are enriched in patients with rapid progression
sec.p: Because the treatment arm did not affect cfDNA or ctDNA features at progression, we next explored whether cfDNA or ctDNA features differ based on clinical response durability. For this, we focused on two clinically informative subgroups from the Alliance A031201 trial. The first comprised 129 patients with rapid progression, defined as reaching the rPFS time within 6 months of randomization, which is indicative of primary resistance to ARPI treatment. The second subgroup included 304 patients with delayed progression, defined a priori as not reaching rPFS until at least 30 months from randomization. Based on the median rPFS in A031201 being 21 to 24 months (25), this delayed progression subgroup had clearly better outcomes and derived clinical benefit from ARPI treatment (Fig. 5A). For longitudinal analysis, there were 63 patients with rapid progression and 72 with delayed progression who had matched baseline and progression cfDNA data (Fig. 5B–D).

sec.p: In both subgroups, the majority of patients displayed a net positive change in cfDNA yields at progression, regardless of whether they received ENZ alone or ENZ + AAP (Fig. 5E and F). Both subgroups also displayed an increase in the fraction of ctDNA-positive patients at progression, regardless of treatment arm (Fig. 5G–J). At baseline, ctDNA-positive patients with rapid progression exhibited a higher burden of genetic alterations across the AR-ctDETECT gene panel compared with those with delayed progression (Fig. 5K), with frequent co-occurrence of multiple alterations (Fig. 5L and M). This higher genetic alteration burden in patients with rapid progression persisted at the progression time point (Fig. 5N–P).

Notably, the only gene with a higher alteration frequency at either time point in patients with delayed progression was AR, which showed a greater prevalence of alterations at progression in the delayed progression subgroup relative to the rapid progression subgroup (Fig. 5N). In contrast, ctDNA from patients with delayed progression was largely devoid of non-AR alterations at both time points (Fig. 5M and P). Together, these findings suggest that non-AR alterations detectable in ctDNA may underlie intrinsic resistance and drive rapid disease progression, whereas AR alterations seem to be essential for disease progression, regardless of treatment durability or timing.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Using longitudinal cfDNA samples from the phase III Alliance A031201 clinical trial (25), we observed an increase in both cfDNA yield and ctDNA positivity at progression compared with baseline in patients receiving first-line ARPI treatment for mCRPC. AR was the most frequently altered gene at both time points, with an increased prevalence of copy-number gains and AR-GSRs at progression. In addition to AR, we identified a higher frequency of copy-number losses at progression in non-AR genes involved in DNA replication and repair (FANCA, POLD1, and RAD54L), cell-cycle regulation and Wnt signaling (CDKN2A and ZNRF3), and transcriptional control (ETS2). The presence of these genetic alterations in mCRPC biopsies (11) supports their relevance as potential contributors to ARPI resistance and as targets for future mechanistic studies.

Prior studies investigating longitudinal changes in ctDNA status have reported inconsistent results, likely due to differences in sampling intervals and assay methods. For instance, one study showed that ctDNA positivity remains relatively stable between first- and second-line ARPI treatment settings, with individual patients showing more pronounced changes in ctDNA fraction with longer intervals between sample collections (50). Furthermore, a conversion from ctDNA-positive at baseline to ctDNA-negative after 4 weeks of ARPI treatment was shown to be associated with longer treatment benefit in the first-line setting (51). In our study of samples collected as part of a randomized phase III trial, we found more conversions from ctDNA-negative to -positive than ctDNA-positive to -negative at progression but no consistent trend in ctDNA aneuploidy fraction changes among patients who were ctDNA-positive at both baseline and progression time points. Although patients in our study had samples collected at progression, differences in the type of progression (node only, bone, and visceral), patient symptoms such as pain, and other adverse clinical features at progression were not considered in this analysis. Future work should consider these variables in the context of the clinical–genetic landscape of treatment resistance and prediction of subsequent therapy outcomes.

Our findings reinforce the central role of AR alterations in mCRPC progression under ARPI pressure. Consistent with previous studies developing liquid classifiers from targeted DNA-seq analysis of AR, the upstream AR enhancer, and non-AR genes in cfDNA, we observed concordant copy-number gains in the AR gene body and AR enhancer, supporting the notion that these regions are usually captured on the same amplicon (6, 50, 52–54). We also confirmed that the burden of AR-GSRs increases at progression (50), especially in patients with delayed rPFS but eventual emergence of acquired resistance to ARPIs. In our previous study, we reported that A031201 patients harboring AR-GSRs at baseline, particularly in the context of an AR ecDNA signature, have worse rPFS and OS (26). The finding that AR ecDNA molecules accumulate multiple AR-GSRs in mCRPC (19, 20), along with a recent study showing that ecDNA accumulates high levels of DNA damage due to transcription–replication conflicts (55), suggests that ecDNA acts as a hotspot for generation of AR-GSRs. Consistent with this, our analyses demonstrated that ctDNA samples displaying the AR ecDNA signature were more likely to harbor LBD-truncating AR-GSRs at higher VAFs than AR-GSRs of unknown significance. Collectively, these observations converge on a model whereby AR ecDNA contributes to acquired resistance via a dual mechanism: it simultaneously (i) increases the AR gene dosage and (ii) accelerates AR gene structural diversification. This process, selected for under ARPI treatment, drives both full-length AR overexpression and the synthesis of truncated, constitutively active AR-Vs (19). The enrichment of these AR ecDNA–associated alterations at progression in both treatment arms of the A031201 trial suggests that AR ecDNA represents a common mechanism of acquired resistance to various ARPI treatments.

In a previous study, we used random survival forest to identify AR and non-AR genetic alterations in A031201 baseline plasma for building a clinical–genomic prognostic model of OS and found that this clinical–genetic prognostic model outperformed a validated clinical prognostic model by nearly 30% (27). In the current study, we stratified patients by two extremes of rPFS to explore alterations in AR and non-AR genes longitudinally in baseline and progression plasma. Although patients with delayed progression (rPFS >30 months) displayed preferential accumulation of AR alterations compared with patients with rapid progression (rPFS <6 months from randomization), the patients with rapid progression displayed an overall higher burden of non-AR genomic alterations at both time points. Many of the patients with rapid progression exhibited concurrent mutation and/or CNAs in these non-AR genes, suggesting reduced AR dependency. These findings are consistent with a previous study showing that ctDNA alterations in genes such as TP53 are associated with a shorter rPFS and may outperform AR alterations for predicting poor ARPI response (56). A distinction between AR-dependent and AR-independent trajectories could inform biomarker-driven patient stratification and support the rationale for combination or novel treatment strategies in patients with AR-independent trajectories, particularly given the high prevalence of TP53 alterations (53, 56–58).

This study has several limitations. First, we used a research-grade AR-ctDETECT assay for cfDNA sequencing without matched tumor or germline DNA. This limits somatic mutation detection, orthogonal validation of genomic alterations in tissue, and the power to differentiate tumor-derived mutations from CH. However, the potential for CH to cause false-positive ctDNA results was low because most samples with potential CH mutations had additional evidence for being ctDNA-positive. Second, the AR-ctDETECT assay targets genomic alterations but does not assess epigenetic, transcriptomic, or proteomic changes that also contribute to resistance in patients with mCRPC (46). Third, this study only takes into consideration the baseline and progression time points, without evaluating intermediate time points. Fourth, not all plasma progression samples were collected on dates that perfectly correspond with clinical or radiographic progression dates. Finally, our findings are specific to patients receiving ENZ with or without AAP as first-line therapy for mCRPC and may not be generalizable to patients who have received other therapies for mCRPC or receive ARPIs for castration-sensitive disease. Future studies are needed to identify ctDNA-based predictors of subsequent proven therapies such as second ARPIs, taxanes, Lu177-PSMA-617, radium-223, or PARP inhibitors with or without ARPIs.

Despite these limitations, our study demonstrates that ctDNA profiling of longitudinal plasma samples from the phase III Alliance A031201 trial can reveal distinct molecular trajectories of resistance to first-line ARPI treatment in mCRPC. AR-driven tumors acquire resistance through the accumulation of gains in the AR gene body and upstream enhancer, as well as AR-GSRs, particularly LBD-truncating AR-GSRs enriched in an ecDNA context. In contrast, rapidly progressing tumors preferentially harbor non-AR alterations at baseline and progression. These findings suggest distinct trajectories of AR-dependent and AR-independent resistance and support the potential for liquid biopsy to enable real-time tracking of tumor evolution and resistance mechanisms. The ability to distinguish these resistance profiles may inform patient eligibility and stratification for future clinical trials or guide the earlier use of non–AR-targeted approaches for patients with AR-independent disease.
